title: Test a small hotel's direct booking path in ten minutes
description:
A small hotel pays a booking site a commission to be introduced to a guest, and pays it again if that guest comes back through the same site. A direct-booking practice helps the hotel get its returning guests to book direct instead.

The first piece of the audit runs from your phone. Pick an independent property with twenty to forty rooms and search for it the way a guest would. Check whether a free link to the hotel's own site shows up beside the booking-site rates; Google shows one for a property connected through a partner, at no charge. Compare the direct rate, then try to finish a direct booking yourself. Whatever breaks is the finding.

That is half an audit. It tells you what is broken, not whether the owner will pay to fix it.

short_name: It Sounds Like Marketing. It's Operations.
title: Getting hotel guests to book direct is operations work
description:
Getting a small hotel's returning guests to book direct sounds like marketing. The work is operations.

At a twenty-room inn, the person who would write the thank-you note is the same person checking in a guest and finding a plumber. The direct path is not a system. It is a list of small jobs, and the list belongs to nobody. A language model can draft the messages and an automation tool can schedule them. Deciding who gets one, and what to tell the owner, is still a person's job.

So the skill is owning a list of small recurring jobs in a business you don't own. Rates and revenue management stay outside the engagement.

title: Where a small hotel's own guest list has to come from
description:
If you build a direct-booking practice for small hotels, one constraint shapes it before any tool does.

Booking.com's own partner help says it doesn't share private guest email addresses. Both sides see an alias ending @guest.booking.com, and partners are asked to keep the conversation on the platform. So you can't win a guest back from the relay address, and you aren't supposed to try.

What the inn needs first is a guest book of its own: a registration card and wifi login that ask for the guest's own email, which the guest chooses to give.

That list falls under US email law, and European rules for European guests. This is not legal advice. Check your jurisdiction and each site's terms.

title: Four numbers that tell you what a small hotel can pay
description:
If you sell a small hotel on getting guests to book direct, price it off four numbers the owner already knows: rooms, average nightly rate, occupancy, and the share of bookings coming through the booking sites.

Those give you the revenue the sites carry. Apply a commission band for the yearly cost. Assume a shift in the mix, and say plainly that the size of that shift is a hypothesis nobody has measured. Subtract what running direct costs. What is left, per month, is the ceiling. Your fee has to sit under it.

On an illustrative twenty-room inn at $180 a night and 70 percent occupancy, the model lands near a thousand to fourteen hundred dollars a month. Some properties can't fund this at all, and the arithmetic tells you which before you quote.
